# On the James and Hilton–Milnor Splittings, & the metastable EHP sequence

**Authors:** Sanath Devalapurkar and Peter Haine

## Abstract

This note provides modern proofs of some classical results in algebraic topology, such as the James Splitting, the Hilton–Milnor Splitting, and the metastable EHP sequence. We prove fundamental splitting results

in the maximal generality of an $\infty$ -category with finite limits and pushouts in which pushouts squares remain pushouts after basechange along an arbitrary morphism (i.e., Mather’s Second Cube Lemma holds). For connected objects, these imply the classical James and Hilton–Milnor Splittings. Moreover, working in this generality shows that the James and Hilton–Milnor splittings hold in many new contexts, for example in: elementary $\infty$ -topoi, profinite spaces, and motivic spaces over arbitrary base schemes. The splitting results in this last context extend Wickelgren and Williams’ splitting result for motivic spaces over a perfect field. We also give two proofs of the metastable EHP sequence in the setting of $\infty$ -topoi: the first is a new, non-computational proof that only utilizes basic connectedness estimates involving the James filtration and the Blakers–Massey Theorem, while the second reduces to the classical computational proof.

## 1. Introduction

A classical result of James shows that given a pointed connected space $X$ , the homotopy type $\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X$ given by suspending the loopspace on the suspension of $X$ splits as a wedge sum

$$ \Sigma\Omega\Sigma X\simeq\bigvee_{i\geq 1}\Sigma X^{\wedge i} $$

of suspensions of smash powers of $X$ [55, 67]. Hilton and Milnor proved a related splitting result [63, 64, 72]: given pointed connected spaces $X$ and $Y$ , they showed that there is a homotopy equivalence

$$ \Omega\Sigma(X\vee Y)\simeq\Omega\Sigma X\times\Omega\Sigma Y\times\Omega\Sigma\left(\bigvee_{i,j\geq 1}X^{\wedge i}\wedge Y^{\wedge j}\right)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

In the classical setting, these splitting results follow from combining a connectedness argument using the hypothesis that $X$ and $Y$ are connected with the following more fundamental splittings: given any pointed spaces $X$ and $Y$ , there are natural equivalences

$$ \Sigma\Omega\Sigma X\simeq\Sigma X\vee(X\wedge\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X)\text{\qquad and\qquad}\Omega(X\vee Y)\simeq\Omega X\times\Omega Y\times\Omega\Sigma(\Omega X\wedge\Omega Y)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

The first objective of this note is to provide clear, modern, and non-computational proofs of these fundamental splittings (1.3). The only property particular to the $\infty$ -category of spaces that our proofs utilize is Mather’s Second Cube Lemma [70]; this asserts that pushout squares remain pushouts after basechange along an arbitrary morphism (see §​ 2.1). Hence these ‘fundamental’ James and Hilton–Milnor Splittings hold in any $\infty$ -category where we can make sense of suspensions, loops, wedge sums, and smash products, and have access to Mather’s Second Cube Lemma:

#### Theorem 1.4 (Fundamental James Splitting; Theorem 2.10).

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with finite limits and pushouts, and assume that Mather’s Second Cube Lemma holds in $\mathcal{X}$ . Then for every pointed object $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ , there is a natural equivalence

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X \displaystyle\simeq\Sigma X\vee(X\wedge\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} n\geq 1 \displaystyle\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X \displaystyle\simeq\left(\bigvee_{1\leq i\leq n}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\right)\vee(X^{\wedge n}\wedge\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

In general, the infinite splitting $\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X\simeq\bigvee_{i\geq 1}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}$ need not hold; roughly speaking, the problem is that if $X$ is not connected, then $(X^{\wedge n}\wedge\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X)$ need not vanish as $n\to\infty$ . However, there is always a natural map $\bigvee_{i\geq 1}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\to\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X$ .

#### Theorem 1.5 (Fundamental Hilton–Milnor Splitting; Theorem 3.1).

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with finite limits and pushouts, and assume that Mather’s Second Cube Lemma holds in $\mathcal{X}$ . Then for every pair of pointed objects $X,Y\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ there is an natural equivalence

$$ \displaystyle\Omega(X\vee Y) \displaystyle\simeq\Omega X\times\Omega Y\times\Omega\Sigma(\Omega X\wedge\Omega Y)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

In §​ 4.2 we explain in what generality the the infinite James Splitting (1.1) and Hilton–Milnor Splitting (1.2) hold, and how to deduce them from Theorems 1.4 and 1.5.

It might seem that knowing that the James and Hilton–Milnor Splittings in this level of generality is of dubious advantage; the settings in which one is most likely to want to apply these splittings are the $\infty$ -category $\mathbf{Spc}$ of spaces (where the results are already known), or an $\infty$ -topos (where the results follows immediately from the results for $\mathbf{Spc}$ ; see §​ 4.2). However, algebraic geometry provides an example that does not immediately follow from the result for spaces: motivic spaces. The obstruction is that the $\infty$ -category of motivic spaces over a scheme is not an $\infty$ -topos; since motivic localization almost never commutes with taking loops, knowing the James and Hilton–Milnor Splittings in the $\infty$ -topos of Nisnevich sheaves does not allow one to deduce that they hold in motivic spaces.

Wickelgren and Williams used the James filtration to prove that the infinite James Splitting (1.1) holds for $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -connected motivic spaces over a perfect field [85, Theorem 1.5]. The reason for the restriction on the base is because their proof relies on Morel’s unstable $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -connectivity Theorem [73, Theorems 5.46 and 6.1], which implies that motivic localization commutes with loops [51, 73]. However, the unstable $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -connectivity property does not hold for higher-dimensional bases [51, 52], so a different method is needed if one wants to prove James and Hilton–Milnor Splittings for motivic spaces over more general bases. This is where our generalization pays off: work of Hoyois [66, Proposition 3.15] shows that, in particular, Mather’s Second Cube Lemma holds in motivic spaces over an arbitrary base scheme. Therefore, Theorems 1.4 and 1.5 apply in this setting. We use these splittings to give a description of the motivic space $\Sigma\Omega\mathbf{P}^{1}$ in terms of wedges of motivic spheres $\mathrm{S}^{i+1,i}$ (Example 2.14), and also give a new description of $\Omega\Sigma(\mathbf{P}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,1,\infty\})$ (Example 3.3). Over a perfect field, we give a new decomposition of $\Omega\Sigma^{2}(\mathbf{P}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,1,\infty\})$ in terms of motivic spheres of the form $\mathrm{S}^{2m+1,m}$ (Example 4.25).

The second goal of this note is to give a modern construction of the metastable EHP sequence in an $\infty$ -topos $\mathcal{X}$ . For every pointed connected object $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ , the James Splitting provides Hopf maps

$$ h_{n}\colon\Omega\Sigma X\to\Omega\Sigma(X^{\wedge n})\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

There is also a James filtration $\{\mathrm{J}_{m}(X)\}_{m\geq 0}$ on $\Omega\Sigma X$ , and, moreover, the composite

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega\Sigma X} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega\Sigma X^{\wedge n}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{n}} $$

is trivial. The sequence (1.6) is not a fiber sequence in general11 1 When $\mathcal{X}$ is the $\infty$ -category of spaces and $X$ is a sphere, James and Toda proved that, roughly, the sequence (1.6) becomes a fiber sequence after $p$ -localization. See [68, 69, 83]for a precise statement., but is in the metastable range:

#### Theorem 1.7 (metastable EHP sequence; Theorem 5.19).

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -topos, $k\geq 0$ an integer, and $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ a pointed $k$ -connected object. Then for each integer $n\geq 1$ , the morphism $\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X)\to\textup{fib}(h_{n})$ is $((n+1)(k+1)-3)$ -connected.

We note here that a morphism is $m$ -connected in our terminology if and only if it is $(m+1)$ -connected in the classical terminology (see Warning 4.9).

We provide two proofs of Theorem 1.7. The first proof is new and non-computational; it only makes use of some basic connectedness estimates involving the James filtration and the Blakers–Massey Theorem. In the second proof we simply note that Theorem 1.7 for a general $\infty$ -topos follows immediately from the claim for the $\infty$ -topos of spaces. In the case of spaces, we provide a computational proof; we include this second proof because we were unable to find the computational proof we were familiar with in the literature.

### 1.1. Linear overview

We have written this note with two audiences in mind: the student interested in seeing proofs of Theorems 1.4, 1.5 and 1.7 in the classical setting of spaces, and the expert homotopy theorist interested in applying these results to more general contexts such as motivic spaces or profinite spaces. The student can always take $\mathcal{X}$ to be the $\infty$ -category of spaces, and the expert can safely skip the background sections provided for the student. We also note that this text should still be accessible to the reader familiar with homotopy (co)limits but unfamiliar with higher categories, since all we use in our proofs are basic manipulations of homotopy (co)limits.

Section 2 is dedicated to proving Theorem 1.4. In §​ 2.1, we provide background on Mather’s Second Cube Lemma and the universality of pushouts. In §​ 2.2, we provide a proof of the James Splitting. Our proof is roughly the same as proofs presented elsewhere [65, 82, 86], but it seems that the generality of the argument we present here is not very well-known.

Section 3 provides a quick proof of Theorem 1.5. Again, shadows of the proof we provide appear in the literature [59, 60, 82], but it seems that the generality of the proof has not been completely internalized by the community. As an application, we use work of Wickelgren [84, Corollary 3.2] to give a new description of the motivic space $\Omega\Sigma(\mathbf{P}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,1,\infty\})$ (Example 3.2).

Section 4 explains how to use a connectedness argument to prove the infinite James Splitting (1.1) and Hilton–Milnor Splitting (1.2) for pointed connected objects of an $\infty$ -topos, and for pointed $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -connected motivic spaces over a perfect field. In §​ 4.1, we begin by recalling the basics of connectedness and the Blakers–Massey Theorem in an $\infty$ -topos; this material is also instrumental in our proof of Theorem 1.7. Subsection 4.2 presents the connectedness argument needed to deduce the infinite splittings and defines the Hopf maps appearing in Theorem 1.7. As an application we give a new description of the motivic space $\Omega\Sigma^{2}(\mathbf{P}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,1,\infty\})$ over a perfect field (Example 4.25).

Section 5 is dedicated to proving Theorem 1.7. In §​ 5.1, we provide the background on the James filtration needed to understand the statement of Theorem 1.7, as well as some connectedness estimates we need to prove Theorem 1.7. In §​ 5.2, we give a refinement of the James Splitting in terms of the James filtration. In §​ 5.3, we first provide a proof of Theorem 1.7 using the Blakers–Massey Theorem (which we have not seen elsewhere), and then record for posterity what we imagine is the standard computational proof of Theorem 1.7.

### 1.2. Notation & background

In this subsection we set the basic notational conventions that we use throughout this note as well as recall a bit of relevant background.

#### Notation 1.8.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category. If $\mathcal{X}$ has a terminal object, we write ${\mathbin{*}}\smallin\mathcal{X}$ for the terminal object and $\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ for the $\infty$ -category of pointed objects in $\mathcal{X}$ . If $\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ has coproducts and $X,Y\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ , we write $X\vee Y$ for the coproduct of $X$ and $Y$ in $\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ . If $\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ has coproducts and products, note that there is a natural comparison morphism $X\vee Y\to X\times Y$ induced by the morphisms

$$ (\operatorname{id}_{X},{\mathbin{*}})\colon X\to X\times Y\text{\qquad and\qquad}({\mathbin{*}},\operatorname{id}_{Y})\colon Y\to X\times Y\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

We say that a morphism $f\colon X\to Y$ in $\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ is null if $f$ factors through the zero object ${\mathbin{*}}$ .

#### Notation 1.9.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with pushouts. Given a span $X\leftarrow W\to Y$ in $\mathcal{X}$ , we write $X\sqcup^{W}Y$ for its pushout.

#### Recollection 1.10.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with finite products and pushouts, and $X,Y\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ pointed objects of $\mathcal{X}$ . The smash product $X\wedge Y$ of $X$ and $Y$ is the cofiber

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\vee Y} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\times Y} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbin{*}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\wedge Y} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ulcorner} $$

of the comparison morphism $X\vee Y\to X\times Y$ .

#### Recollection 1.11.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with pushouts and a terminal object. The suspension of an object $X\smallin\mathcal{X}$ is the pushout

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbin{*}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbin{*}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma X\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ulcorner} $$

#### Recollection 1.12.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with finite limits. The loop object of a pointed object $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ is the pullback

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega X} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbin{*}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbin{*}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner} $$

in $\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ .

We also make repeated use of the following easy fact. The unfamiliar reader should consult [53, 75].

#### Lemma 1.13.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with pushouts and

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{1}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{0}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X_{2}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W_{1}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W_{0}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W_{2}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y_{1}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y_{0}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y_{2}} $$

a commutative diagram in $\mathcal{X}$ . Then the colimit of the diagram (1.14) exists and is equivalent to both of the following two iterated pushouts:

- (1.13.1) Form the pushout of the rows of (1.14), then take the pushout of the resulting span ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\displaystyle X_{1}\operatornamewithlimits{\sqcup}^{X_{0}}X_{2}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\displaystyle W_{1}\operatornamewithlimits{\sqcup}^{W_{0}}W_{2}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\displaystyle Y_{1}\operatornamewithlimits{\sqcup}^{Y_{0}}Y_{2}\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss}}$

- (1.13.2) Form the pushout of the columns of (1.14), then take the pushout of the resulting span ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\displaystyle X_{1}\operatornamewithlimits{\sqcup}^{W_{1}}Y_{1}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\displaystyle X_{0}\operatornamewithlimits{\sqcup}^{W_{0}}Y_{0}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\displaystyle X_{2}\operatornamewithlimits{\sqcup}^{W_{2}}Y_{2}\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss}}$

## 2. The James Splitting

In this section, we present a proof of the James Splitting which holds in any $\infty$ -category with finite limits and pushouts, where pushout squares remain pushouts after basechange along an arbitrary morphism. The argument we give roughly follows the argument Hopkins gave in his course on stable homotopy theory in the setting of spaces [65, Lecture 4, §3]; Hopkins attributes this proof to James [67, 68, 69]and Ganea [58].

### 2.1. Universal pushouts and Mather’s Second Cube Lemma

The key property utilized in the proofs we present of the James and Hilton–Milnor Splittings is that pushout squares are preserved by arbitrary basechange. This implies that, in particular, the James and Hilton–Milnor Splittings hold in any $\infty$ -topos, but also in other situations (such as motivic spaces). In this subsection, we provide the categorical context that we work in for the rest of the paper and give a convenient reformulation of the stability of pullbacks under basechange in terms of Mather’s Second Cube Lemma (Lemma 2.6).

#### Recollection 2.1.

Let $\mathcal{I}$ be an $\infty$ -category and let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with pullbacks and all $\mathcal{I}$ -shaped colimits. We say that $\mathcal{I}$ -shaped colimits in $\mathcal{X}$ are universal if $\mathcal{I}$ -shaped colimits in $\mathcal{X}$ are stable under pullback along any morphism. That is, for every diagram $F\colon\mathcal{I}\to\mathcal{X}$ and pair of morphisms $\operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{i\smallin\mathcal{I}}F(i)\to Z$ and $Y\to Z$ in $\mathcal{X}$ , the natural morphism

$$ \operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{i\smallin\mathcal{I}}(F(i)\times_{Z}Y)\to\Big(\operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{i\smallin\mathcal{I}}F(i)\Big)\times_{Z}Y $$

is an equivalence.

#### Example 2.2.

Let $0\leq n\leq\infty$ , and let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $n$ -topos. One of the Giraud–Lurie axioms for $n$ -topoi guarentees that all small colimits in $\mathcal{X}$ are universal [44, Theorem 6.1.0.6 & Proposition 6.4.1.5]. In particular, small colimits in the category $\mathbf{Set}$ of sets and the $\infty$ -category $\mathbf{Spc}$ of spaces are universal.

#### Example 2.3.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an elementary $\infty$ -topos in the sense of [77, Definition 3.5]. Then all colimits that exist in $\mathcal{X}$ are universal [77, Corollary 3.12]. In particular, finite colimits are universal in $\mathcal{X}$ .

#### Example 2.4 (motivic spaces).

Let $S$ be a scheme. The $\infty$ -category $\mathbf{H}(S)$ of motivic spaces over $S$ is defined as the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -localization of the $\infty$ -topos $\operatorname{Sh}_{\Nis}(\mathbf{Sm}_{S})$ of sheaves of spaces on the category $\mathbf{Sm}_{S}$ of smooth schemes of finite type over $S$ equipped with the Nisnevich topology. Concretely, $\mathbf{H}(S)$ is the full subcategory of $\operatorname{Sh}_{\Nis}(\mathbf{Sm}_{S})$ spanned by those Nisnevich sheaves $\mathcal{F}$ on $\mathbf{Sm}_{S}$ with the property that for each smooth $S$ -scheme $X$ , the projection $\pr_{1}\colon X\times_{S}\mathbf{A}_{S}^{1}\to X$ induces an equivalence

$$ \pr_{1}^{{\mathbin{*}}}\colon\mathcal{F}(X)\similarrightarrow\mathcal{F}(X\times_{S}\mathbf{A}_{S}^{1})\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

The inclusion $\mathbf{H}(S)\subset\operatorname{Sh}_{\Nis}(\mathbf{Sm}_{S})$ admits a left adjoint $\Lmot\colon\operatorname{Sh}_{\Nis}(\mathbf{Sm}_{S})\to\mathbf{H}(S)$ called motivic localization. Motivic localization preserves finite products, but not all finite limits. Moreover, the $\infty$ -category $\mathbf{H}(S)$ is not an $\infty$ -topos (see [81, 76]), and it is not immediately clear from the construction if any colimits are universal in $\mathbf{H}(S)$ . Nonetheless, Hoyois has shown that all small colimits are universal in $\mathbf{H}(S)$ [66, Proposition 3.15].

#### Example 2.5 (profinite spaces).

We say that a space $X$ is $\mathrm{\pi}$ -finite if $X$ is truncated, has finitely many connected components, and $\mathrm{\pi}_{i}(X,x)$ is finite for every integer $i\geq 1$ and point $x\smallin X$ . Write $\mathbf{Spc}_{\mathrm{\pi}}\subset\mathbf{Spc}$ for the full subcategory spanned by the $\mathrm{\pi}$ -finite spaces and $\Pro(\mathbf{Spc}_{\mathrm{\pi}})$ for the $\infty$ -category of profinite spaces. Infinite coproducts in $\Pro(\mathbf{Spc}_{\mathrm{\pi}})$ are not universal [46, Warning E.6.0.9], however, finite colimits and geometric realizations of simplicial objects are universal in $\Pro(\mathbf{Spc}_{\mathrm{\pi}})$ [46, Theorem E.6.3.1 & Corollary E.6.3.2].

The following result gives a reformulation of what it means for pushouts to be universal in terms of Mather’s Second Cube Lemma, which Mather originally proved in the $\infty$ -category of spaces [70, Theorem 25]. See [47, Tag 011H] for an elegant proof of Mather’s Second Cube Lemma in $\mathbf{Spc}$ .

#### Lemma 2.6.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with pullbacks and pushouts. The following conditions are equivalent:

- (2.6.1) Pushouts in $\mathcal{X}$ are universal.

- (2.6.2) Mather’s Second Cube Lemma holds in $\mathcal{X}$ : Given a commutative cube ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{0}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{3}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{0}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{3}}$ in $\mathcal{X}$ where the bottom horizontal face is a pushout square and all vertical faces are pullback squares, then the top horizontal square is a pushout square.

#### Proof.

The implication (2.6.1) $\Rightarrow$ (2.6.2) is immediate. To see that (2.6.2) $\Rightarrow$ (2.6.1), suppose that we are given a pushout square

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{0}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{3}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ulcorner} $$

in $\mathcal{X}$ and morphisms $f\colon B_{3}\to Z$ and $g\colon Y\to Z$ in $\mathcal{X}$ . For each $i\smallin\{0,1,2,3\}$ , define $A_{i}\coloneq B_{i}\times_{Z}Y$ , so that all the vertical squares in the diagram

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{0}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{3}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{0}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{3}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f} $$

are pullbacks. Since the bottom horizontal square of the cube in (2.8) is a pushout, (2.6.2) implies that the top horizontal square is also a pushout. Thus the pushout square (2.7) remains a pushout after base change along an arbitrary morphism, as desired. ∎

Since the main results of this note are about pointed objects, we make the following mildly abusive convention:

#### Convention 2.9.

We say that an $\infty$ -category $\mathcal{X}$ has universal pushouts if $\mathcal{X}$ has finite limits and pushouts, and pushouts in $\mathcal{X}$ are universal.

### 2.2. Statement of the James Splitting & Consequences

The James Splitting, originally proven in [67], provides a splitting of the space $\Omega\Sigma X$ after a single suspension. The goal of this subsection is to provide a proof of the James Splitting that only relies on the universality of pushouts and a few elementary computations involving the interaction between forming suspensions, loop objects, and smash products.

#### Theorem 2.10 (Fundamental James Splitting).

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with universal pushouts. For every pointed object $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ , there is a natural equivalence

$$ \Sigma\Omega\Sigma X\simeq\Sigma X\vee\Sigma(X\wedge\Omega\Sigma X)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

Using the fact that $\Sigma(X\wedge\Omega\Sigma X)\simeq X\wedge\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X$ (Lemma 2.26) and iterating the equivalence of Theorem 2.10, we see:

#### Corollary 2.11 (Fundamental James Splitting, redux).

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with universal pushouts. For each pointed object $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ and integer $n\geq 1$ , there is a natural equivalence

$$ \Sigma\Omega\Sigma X\simeq\left(\bigvee_{1\leq i\leq n}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\right)\vee(X^{\wedge n}\wedge\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

#### Notation 2.12.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with universal pushouts and $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ a pointed object. Assume that $\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ has countable coproducts. Passing to the colimit as $n\to\infty$ , the coproduct insertions

$$ \bigvee_{i=1}^{n}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\to\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X $$

provided by Corollary 2.11 provide a natural comparison morphism

$$ \bigvee_{i=1}^{\infty}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\to\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X\hbox to0.0pt{\ ,\hss} $$

which we denote by $c_{X}\colon\bigvee_{i=1}^{\infty}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\to\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X$ .

#### Warning 2.13.

The comparison morphism $c_{X}$ need not be an equivalence. For example, if $\mathcal{X}=\mathbf{Spc}$ and $X=\mathrm{S}^{0}$ is the $0$ -sphere, then the map

$$ c_{\mathrm{S}^{0}}\colon\bigvee_{i=1}^{\infty}\mathrm{S}^{1}\to\Sigma\Omega\Sigma\mathrm{S}^{0}\simeq\bigvee_{i\smallin\mathbf{Z}}\mathrm{S}^{1} $$

is not an equivalence. Even though both the source and target of $c_{\mathrm{S}^{0}}$ are both countable wedges of copies of $\mathrm{S}^{1}$ , the map $c_{\mathrm{S}^{0}}$ is the summand inclusion induced by the inclusion $\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 1}\subset\mathbf{Z}$ .

We analyze when the comparison morphism $c_{X}$ is an equivalence in §​ 4.2.

#### Example 2.14.

Let $S$ be a scheme. Since colimits are universal in the $\infty$ -category $\mathbf{H}(S)$ of motivic spaces over $S$ (Example 2.4), Theorem 2.10 implies that for any pointed motivic space $X\smallin\mathbf{H}(S)_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ and integer $n\geq 1$ , we have $\mathrm{S}^{1}$ -James Splittings

$$ \Sigma\Omega\Sigma X\simeq\left(\bigvee_{1\leq i\leq n}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\right)\vee(X^{\wedge n}\wedge\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

Write $\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}$ for the multiplicative group scheme over $S$ . Since $\Sigma\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}\simeq\mathbf{P}_{S}^{1}$ , setting $X=\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}$ we see that

#### Remark 2.16.

There is another suspension in motivic homotopy theory, given by smashing with the multiplicative group scheme $\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}$ . One would like an analogue of the James Splitting in $\mathbf{H}(S)_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ for $\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}$ -suspensions. For $S=\spec(\mathbf{R})$ , Betti realization defines a functor $\mathbf{H}(\spec(\mathbf{R}))\to\mathbf{Spc}_{\mathrm{C}_{2}}$ to $\mathrm{C}_{2}$ -spaces which sends $\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}$ to the sign representation circle $\mathrm{S}^{\mathrm{\sigma}}$ and $\mathrm{S}^{1}$ to the circle with trivial $\mathrm{C}_{2}$ -action. Even though Betti realization is not an equivalence, it closely ties $\mathbf{R}$ -motivic homotopy theory with $\mathrm{C}_{2}$ -equivariant homotopy theory. In [62], Hill studies the signed James construction in $\mathrm{C}_{2}$ -equivariant unstable homotopy theory, and shows that an analogue of the James Splitting holds for $\Omega^{\mathrm{\sigma}}\Sigma^{\mathrm{\sigma}}X$ after suspending by the regular representation sphere $\mathrm{S}^{\mathrm{\rho}}=\mathrm{S}^{1}\wedge\mathrm{S}^{\mathrm{\sigma}}$ . This might lead one to hope that there is an analogue of Hill’s result in motivic homotopy theory which proves the James Splitting for $\Omega_{\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}}\Sigma_{\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}}X$ after $\mathbf{P}^{1}$ -suspension; at the moment, we are not aware of such a result.

## 3. The Hilton–Milnor Splitting

The main result of this section is the following:

#### Theorem 3.1 (Fundamental Hilton–Milnor Splitting).

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with universal pushouts and $X,Y\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ . Then there is a natural equivalence

$$ \Omega(X\vee Y)\simeq\Omega X\times\Omega Y\times\Omega\Sigma(\Omega X\wedge\Omega Y)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

Before giving the proof of Theorem 3.1, we discuss some applications.

#### Example 3.2.

Let $S$ be a scheme. Since colimits are universal in the $\infty$ -category $\mathbf{H}(S)$ of motivic spaces over $S$ (Example 2.4), Theorem 3.1 implies that for any pointed motivic spaces $X,Y\smallin\mathbf{H}(S)_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ we have an equivalence

$$ \Omega(X\vee Y)\simeq\Omega X\times\Omega Y\times\Omega\Sigma(\Omega X\wedge\Omega Y)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

The Hilton–Milnor Splitting allows us to give a new description of the motivic space $\Omega\Sigma(\mathbf{P}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,1,\infty\})$ :

#### Example 3.3.

Let $S$ be a quasicompact quasiseparated scheme. Write $\{0,1,\infty\}\subset\mathbf{P}_{S}^{1}$ for the closed subscheme given by the union of the images of the closed embeddings $S\hookrightarrow\mathbf{P}_{S}^{1}$ at $0$ , $1$ , and $\infty$ , respectively. Using the Morel–Voevodsky motivic purity Theorem [50, 66, 74], Wickelgren [84, Corollary 3.2] showed that there is an equivalence

$$ \Sigma(\mathbf{P}_{S}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,1,\infty\})\simeq\Sigma(\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}\vee\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}) $$

in the $\infty$ -category $\mathbf{H}(S)_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ . Since $\Sigma\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}\simeq\mathbf{P}_{S}^{1}$ , setting $X=Y=\Sigma\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}$ in Example 3.2 we see that there are equivalences

$$ \displaystyle\Omega\Sigma(\mathbf{P}_{S}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,1,\infty\}) \displaystyle\simeq\Omega\Sigma(\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}\vee\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}) \displaystyle\simeq\Omega\Sigma\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}\times\Omega\Sigma\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}\times\Omega\Sigma(\Omega\Sigma\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}\wedge\Omega\Sigma\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}) \displaystyle\simeq\Omega\mathbf{P}_{S}^{1}\times\Omega\mathbf{P}_{S}^{1}\times\Omega\Sigma(\Omega\mathbf{P}_{S}^{1}\wedge\Omega\mathbf{P}_{S}^{1})\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

Applying the James Splitting of Example 2.14 we see that for each integer $n\geq 1$ , we can also express $\Omega\Sigma(\mathbf{P}_{S}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,1,\infty\})$ as

$$ \Omega\Sigma(\mathbf{P}_{S}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,1,\infty\})\simeq\Omega\mathbf{P}_{S}^{1}\times\Omega\mathbf{P}_{S}^{1}\times\Omega\left(\left(\bigvee_{1\leq i\leq n}\Omega\mathbf{P}_{S}^{1}\wedge\mathrm{S}^{i+1,i}\right)\vee\left(\mathrm{S}^{n+1,n}\wedge(\Omega\mathbf{P}_{S}^{1})^{\wedge 2}\right)\right)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

We now turn to the proof of the Hilton–Milnor Splitting. We first show that there is a fiber sequence

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma(\Omega Y\wedge\Omega X)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\vee Y} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\times Y\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss}} $$

We then show that the sequence (3.4) splits after taking loops. To do this, we construct a section

$$ \Omega(X\times Y)\to\Omega(X\vee Y)\hbox to0.0pt{\ ,\hss} $$

and use the fact that a fiber sequence of group objects with a section splits on the level of underlying objects. After proving that (3.4) is a fiber sequence we give a quick review of group objects and deduce Theorem 3.1 from the Splitting Lemma (Lemma 3.12).

We start with the following observation:

#### Lemma 3.5.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with finite limits and $X,Y\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ . Then there is a natural equivalence

$$ \textup{fib}((\operatorname{id}_{X},{\mathbin{*}})\colon X\to X\times Y)\simeq\Omega Y\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

Next, we prove the existence of the fiber sequence (3.4).

#### Lemma 3.6.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with universal pushouts and $X,Y\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ . Then there is a natural equivalence

$$ \textup{fib}(X\vee Y\to X\times Y)\simeq\Sigma(\Omega Y\wedge\Omega X)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

#### Proof.

Write $F\coloneq\textup{fib}(X\vee Y\to X\times Y)$ . By Proposition 2.21, it suffices to show that there is a pushout square

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega Y\times\Omega X} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega X} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega Y} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pr_{2}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pr_{1}} $$

The bottom horizontal square in (3.7) is a pushout square by definition, so the assumption that pushouts in $\mathcal{X}$ are universal implies that the top horizontal square is a pushout as well. ∎

### 3.1. Reminder on group objects & the Splitting Lemma

In order to split the fiber sequence (3.4) after taking loops, we need a few basic facts about group objects (also called $\mathbf{E}_{1}$ -groups or grouplike $\mathbf{E}_{1}$ -algebras) in $\infty$ -categories, which we now review. We begin with a little motivation for the definition of group objects as deloopings. For the genesis of these ideas, we refer the reader to [48, 78, 79]. The reader should consult [45, §§4.1.2 & 5.2.6] for a modern treatment.

#### Notation 3.8.

We write $\mathbf{\Delta}$ for the category of nonempty linearly ordered finite sets. As usual, given a simplicial object $X\colon\mathbf{\Delta}^{\op}\to\mathcal{X}$ , we write $X_{n}\coloneq X([n])$ for the $n$ -simplices of $X$ .

Recall that the bar construction is a fully faithful functor from the category of monoids to the category of simplicial sets. The essential image of the bar construction consists of those simplicial sets $X\colon\mathbf{\Delta}^{\op}\to\mathbf{Set}$ satisfying the following conditions:

- (1) We have $X_{0}\simeq{\mathbin{*}}$ .

- (2) Segal condition: For each $n>0$ and $t\smallin[n]$ , the square ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X([n])}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X(\{t<\cdots<n\})}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X(\{0<\cdots<t\})}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X(\{t\})}$ is a pullback square.

The face map $d_{1}\colon X_{1}\times X_{1}\simeq X_{2}\to X_{1}$ provides a multiplication on $X_{1}$ with unit given by the degeneracy map $s_{0}\colon{\mathbin{*}}\simeq X_{0}\to X_{1}$ .

Since groups form a full subcategory of the category of monoids, the bar construction also identifies the category of groups with a full subcategory of the category of simplicial sets. For this it is better to use an alternative characterization of the existence of inverses: a monoid $M$ is a group if and only if the shear maps

$$ \displaystyle M\times M \displaystyle\to M\times M\text{\qquad and\qquad}M\times M\to M\times M \displaystyle(m,n) \displaystyle\mapsto(m,mn)\phantom{\text{\qquad and\qquad}}(m,n)\mapsto(mn,n) $$

are bijections. Translating this into simplicial sets one sees that the category of groups is equivalent to the full subcategory of $\Fun(\mathbf{\Delta}^{\op},\mathbf{Set})$ spanned by the simplicial sets $X$ satisfying (1), (2), and:

- (3) The induced squares ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X(\{0<1<2\})}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X(\{0<2\})}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X(\{0<1\})}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X(\{0\})}$ $\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces d_{1}}$ $\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces d_{2}}$ and ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X(\{0<1<2\})}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X(\{0<2\})}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X(\{1<2\})}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X(\{0\})}$ $\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces d_{1}}$ $\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces d_{0}}$ are pullback squares.

We emphasize that condition (3) is not implied by the Segal condition (2).

The following is the correct generalization of a group object in an arbitrary $\infty$ -category. The point is to replace the Segal condition with a stronger condition that also encompasses condition (3). See [44].

#### Definition 3.9.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category. A group object in $\mathcal{X}$ is a simplicial object $G\colon\mathbf{\Delta}^{\op}\to\mathcal{X}$ such that:

- (3.9.1) The object $G_{0}$ is a terminal object of $\mathcal{X}$ .

- (3.9.2) For each object $S\smallin\mathbf{\Delta}^{\op}$ and partition $S=T\cup T^{\prime}$ such that $T\cap T^{\prime}=\{t\}$ consists of a single element, the induced square ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G(S)}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G(T^{\prime})}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G(T)}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces G(\{t\})}$ is a pullback square in $\mathcal{X}$ .

In this case, we call $G_{1}\smallin\mathcal{X}$ the underlying object of $G$ . We often identify a group object by its underlying object. We write $\Grp(\mathcal{X})\subset\Fun(\mathbf{\Delta}^{\op},\mathcal{X})$ for the full subcategory spanned by the group objects.

The key example of a group object is loops on a pointed object. As a simplicial object, $\Omega X$ can be written as the Čech nerve of the basepoint ${\mathbin{*}}\to X$ ; since we use Čech nerves in §​ 4.1, we recall the definition here.

#### Recollection 3.10.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with pullbacks, and let $e\colon W\to X$ be a morphism in $\mathcal{X}$ . The Čech nerve $\Cech(e)$ of $e$ is the simplicial object

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\displaystyle W\operatornamewithlimits{\times}_{X}W\operatornamewithlimits{\times}_{X}W} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\displaystyle W\operatornamewithlimits{\times}_{X}W} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W} $$

in $\mathcal{X}$ . Here $\Cech(e)_{n}$ is the $(n+1)$ -fold fiber product of $W$ over $X$ , each degeneracy map is a diagonal morphism, and each face map is a projection. Note that the morphism $e\colon W\to X$ defines a natural augmentation $\Cech(e)\to X$ .

#### Lemma 3.11.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with finite limits and $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ . Then $\Omega X$ naturally admits the structure of a group object of $\mathcal{X}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\mathrm{U}(X)$ denote the Čech nerve of the basepoint ${\mathbin{*}}\to X$ . ## 4. Connectedness & the James Splitting

The purpose of this section is explain how to use a connectedness argument to show that if $X$ is a pointed connected object of an $\infty$ -topos, then the comparison morphism

$$ c_{X}\colon\bigvee_{i=1}^{\infty}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\to\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X $$

is an equivalence. To do this, we start by reviewing the basics of connectedness in an $\infty$ -topos (§​ 4.1). We also prove some basic connectedness results that we need in our proof of the metastable EHP sequence in Section 5. Subsection 4.2 proves the infinite James and Hilton–Milnor Splittings for connected objects and explains how to deduce Wickelgren and William’s James Splitting in motivic spaces over a perfect field from these results.

### 4.1. Connectedness and the Blakers–Massey Theorem

In this subsection, we review the basic properties of $k$ -truncated and $k$ -connected morphisms in an $\infty$ -topos. We also recall the Blakers–Massey Theorem (Theorem 4.15) and Freudenthal Suspension Theorem (Corollary 4.16) in an $\infty$ -topos, since our proof of the metastable EHP sequence in §​ 5 relies on these results.

The reader interested in the details of the results reviewed here should consult [44, 49]for connectedness results, and [49] for the Blakers–Massey Theorem.

#### Definition 4.1.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -topos. For each integer $k\geq-2$ , define $k$ -truncatedness for morphisms in $\mathcal{X}$ recursively as follows.

- (4.1.1) A morphism $f$ is $(-2)$ -truncated if $f$ is an equivalence.

- (4.1.2) For $k\geq-1$ , a morphism $f\colon X\to Y$ is $k$ -truncated if the diagonal $\Delta_{f}\colon X\to X\times_{Y}X$ is $(k-1)$ -truncated.

An object $X\smallin\mathcal{X}$ is $k$ -truncated if the unique morphism $X\to{\mathbin{*}}$ is $k$ -truncated.

Write $\mathcal{X}_{\leq k}\subset\mathcal{X}$ for the full subcategory spanned by the $k$ -truncated objects. The inclusion $\mathcal{X}_{\leq k}\subset\mathcal{X}$ admits a left adjoint which we denote by $\trun_{\leq k}\colon\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{X}_{\leq k}$ .

#### Example 4.2.

Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a small $\infty$ -category equipped with a Grothendieck topology $\tau$ , and let $k\geq-2$ be an integer. Then a sheaf $\mathcal{F}\smallin\operatorname{Sh}_{\tau}(\mathcal{C})$ of spaces on $\mathcal{C}$ with respect to $\tau$ is $k$ -truncated if and only if $\mathcal{F}(c)$ is a $k$ -truncated space for every $c\smallin\mathcal{C}$ . That is, $\mathcal{F}$ is $k$ -truncated if and only if $\mathcal{F}$ is a sheaf of $k$ -truncated spaces.

#### Remark 4.3.

If $\mathcal{X}$ is an $\infty$ -topos, then the full subcategory $\mathcal{X}_{\leq 0}$ spanned by the $0$ -truncated objects is an ordinary topos, i.e., a category of sheaves of sets on a Grothendieck site.

#### Recollection 4.4.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -topos. A morphism $f\colon X\to Y$ in $\mathcal{X}$ is an effective epimorphism if the augmentation $\Cech(f)\to Y$ exhibits $Y$ as the colimit of the Čech nerve of $f$ (see Recollection 3.10). Equivalently, $f$ is an effective epimorphism if and only if $\trun_{\leq 0}(f)\colon\trun_{\leq 0}(X)\to\trun_{\leq 0}(Y)$ is an effective epimorphism in the ordinary topos $\mathcal{X}_{\leq 0}$ of $0$ -truncated objects of $\mathcal{X}$ [44, Proposition 7.2.1.14].

#### Example 4.5.

A morphism $f\colon X\to Y$ in the $\infty$ -topos $\mathbf{Spc}$ of spaces is an effective epimorphism if and only if $\mathrm{\pi}_{0}(f)\colon\mathrm{\pi}_{0}(X)\to\mathrm{\pi}_{0}(Y)$ is a surjection of sets.

#### Definition 4.6.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -topos. For each integer $k\geq-2$ , define $k$ -connectedness for morphisms in $\mathcal{X}$ recursively as follows.

- (4.6.1) Every morphism is $(-2)$ -connected.

- (4.6.2) For $k\geq-1$ , a morphism $f\colon X\to Y$ is $k$ -connected if $f$ is an effective epimorphism and the diagonal $\Delta_{f}\colon X\to X\times_{Y}X$ is $(k-1)$ -connected.

A morphism $f$ is $\infty$ -connected if $f$ is $k$ -connected for all $k\geq-2$ .

An object $X\smallin\mathcal{X}$ is $k$ -connected if the unique morphism $X\to{\mathbin{*}}$ is $k$ -connected.

#### Remark 4.7.

A morphism $f$ is $(-1)$ -connected if and only if $f$ is an effective epimorphism.

#### Definition 4.8.

An $\infty$ -topos $\mathcal{X}$ is hypercomplete if every $\infty$ -connected morphism in $\mathcal{X}$ is an equivalence.

#### Warning 4.9.

Our conventions for connectedness follow those of Anel, Biedermann, Finster, and Joyal [49, §3.3]. For $k\geq 0$ , a homotopy type $X$ is $k$ -connected in our sense if and only if $X$ is $k$ -connected in the classical terminology [56, 61, 71]. In particular, $X$ is $0$ -connected if and only if $X$ is path-connected. This convention differs from the classical one for maps: an $n$ -connected map in our sense is an $(n+1)$ -connected map in the classical sense.

Comparing to Lurie’s terminology [44, §6.5.1], an object or morphism is $n$ -connected in our sense if and only if it is $(n+1)$ -connective in Lurie’s sense. One of the benefits of our terminological choice is that the constant factors in many connectedness estimates are eliminated (see Theorems 4.15 and 4.16).

The following basic properties of $k$ -connected morphisms are proven in [44, §6.5.1].

#### Proposition 4.10.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -topos and $k\geq-2$ be an integer. Then:

- (4.10.1) The class of $k$ -connected morphisms in $\mathcal{X}$ is stable under composition.

- (4.10.2) The class of $k$ -connected morphisms in $\mathcal{X}$ is stable under pushout along any morphism.

- (4.10.3) The class of $k$ -connected morphisms in $\mathcal{X}$ is stable under pullback along any morphism.

- (4.10.4) The class of $k$ -connected objects in $\mathcal{X}$ is stable under finite products.

- (4.10.5) Given morphisms $f\colon X\to Y$ and $g\colon Y\to Z$ in $\mathcal{X}$ where $f$ is $k$ -connected, the morphism $g$ is $k$ -connected if and only if $gf$ is $k$ -connected.

- (4.10.6) Given a morphism $f\colon X\to Y$ in $\mathcal{X}$ with a section $s\colon Y\to X$ , the morphism $f$ is $(k+1)$ -connected if and only if the section $s$ is $k$ -connected.

- (4.10.7) An object $X\smallin\mathcal{X}$ is $k$ -connected if and only if the $k$ -truncation $\trun_{\leq k}(X)$ of $X$ is terminal in $\mathcal{X}$ .

Since the $k$ -truncation functor $\trun_{\leq k}\colon\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{X}$ preserves filtered colimits, from (4.10.7) we deduce:

#### Corollary 4.11.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -topos and $k\geq-2$ be an integer. Then the class of $k$ -connected objects of $\mathcal{X}$ is stable under filtered colimits.

In the $\infty$ -topos of spaces, the following connectedness estimates are usually done by appealing to cell structures. Such arguments are unavailable in an arbitrary $\infty$ -topos, so we deduce these connectedness estimates from Proposition 4.10.

#### Proposition 4.12.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -topos, $X,Y\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ pointed objects, and $k,\ell\geq 0$ integers. If $X$ is $k$ -connected and $Y$ is $\ell$ -connected, then:

- (4.12.1) The suspension $\Sigma X$ is $(k+1)$ -connected.

- (4.12.2) The coproduct insertion $X\to X\vee Y$ is $(\ell-1)$ -connected.

- (4.12.3) The natural morphism $X\vee Y\to X\times Y$ is $(k+\ell)$ -connected.

- (4.12.4) The smash product $X\wedge Y$ is $(k+\ell+1)$ -connected.

- (4.12.5) For each postive integer $n$ , the $n$ -fold smash product $X^{\wedge n}$ is $(n(k+1)-1)$ -connected.

#### Proof.

For (4.12.1) note that since $k$ -connected morphisms are stable under pushout (4.10.2), the definition of the suspension $\Sigma X$ as a pushout shows that the basepoint ${\mathbin{*}}\to\Sigma X$ is $k$ -connected. Hence $\Sigma X$ is $(k+1)$ -connected (4.10.6).

Second, (4.12.2) follows from the fact that the basepoint ${\mathbin{*}}\to Y$ is $(\ell-1)$ -connected (4.10.6), combined with the fact that $(\ell-1)$ -connected morphisms are stable under pushout (4.10.2). Third, (4.12.3) follows from the fact that the basepoints ${\mathbin{*}}\to X$ and ${\mathbin{*}}\to Y$ are $(k-1)$ -connected and $(\ell-1)$ -connected (4.10.6), respectively, and a general fact about pushout-products of connected morphisms [49, Corollary 3.3.7(4)].

Now we prove (4.12.4). Since $(k+\ell)$ -connected morphisms are stable under pushout (4.10.2), by (4.12.1) and the pushout square

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\vee Y} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\times Y} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbin{*}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\wedge Y} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ulcorner} $$

defining the smash product $X\wedge Y$ , we see that the basepoint ${\mathbin{*}}\to X\wedge Y$ is $(k+\ell)$ -connected. Hence $X\wedge Y$ is $(k+\ell+1)$ -connected (4.10.6).

Finally, (4.12.5) follows from (4.12.4) by induction. ∎

Now we record a convenient fact about the interaction between connectedness and pullbacks that we need in out proof of the metastable EHP sequence.

#### Proposition 4.13.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -topos, $\ell\geq-2$ be an integer, and

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C^{\prime}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B^{\prime}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g^{\prime}} $$

be a commutative diagram in $\mathcal{X}$ . If $a$ and $b$ are $\ell$ -connected and $c$ is $(\ell+1)$ -connected, then the induced morphism on pullbacks $a\times_{c}b\colon A\times_{C}B\to A^{\prime}\times_{C^{\prime}}B^{\prime}$ is $\ell$ -connected.

#### Proof.

Since $\ell$ -connected morphisms are stable under composition, by factoring the induced morphism $A\times_{C}B\to A^{\prime}\times_{C^{\prime}}B^{\prime}$ as a composite of induced morphisms

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\times_{C}B} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}\times_{C^{\prime}}B} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}\times_{C^{\prime}}B^{\prime}\hbox to0.0pt{\ ,\hss}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a\,\times_{c}\operatorname{id}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\operatorname{id}\times_{\operatorname{id}}b} $$

it suffices to prove the claim in the special case $B=B^{\prime}$ and the morphism $b\colon B\to B^{\prime}$ is the identity. To prove the claim when $b$ is the identity, first write $(\operatorname{id}_{A},f)\colon A\to A\times_{C^{\prime}}C$ for the section of the projection $A\times_{C^{\prime}}C\to A$ induced by the commutative square

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C^{\prime}\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}a} $$

Consider the following commutative diagram of pullback squares

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\times_{C}B} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\times_{C^{\prime}}B} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}\times_{C^{\prime}}B} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A\times_{C^{\prime}}C} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}\times_{C^{\prime}}C} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C^{\prime}\hbox to0.0pt{\ ,\hss}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\operatorname{id}_{A},f)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}} $$

and notice that the composite middle horizontal map $A\to C$ is $f$ . Since $c\colon C\to C^{\prime}$ is $(\ell+1)$ -connected, the projection $A\times_{C^{\prime}}C\to A$ is $(\ell+1)$ -connected (4.10.3). Hence the section $(\operatorname{id}_{A},f)\colon A\to A\times_{C^{\prime}}C$ is $\ell$ -connected (4.10.6). Consequently, the induced morphism $A\times_{C}B\to A\times_{C^{\prime}}B$ is $\ell$ -connected. Now note that since $a\colon A\to A^{\prime}$ is $\ell$ -connected, the induced morphism $A\times_{C^{\prime}}B\to A^{\prime}\times_{C^{\prime}}B$ is $\ell$ -connected. Hence the composite morphism $A\times_{C}B\to A^{\prime}\times_{C^{\prime}}B$ is $\ell$ -connected, as desired. ∎

In particular, Proposition 4.13 shows that the class of $\ell$ -connected morphisms in an $\infty$ -topos is closed under finite products. Setting $B=B^{\prime}={\mathbin{*}}$ in Proposition 4.13 we deduce:

#### Corollary 4.14.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -topos, $\ell\geq-2$ be an integer, and

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A^{\prime}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C^{\prime}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces a} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}} $$

be a commutative square in $\mathcal{X}$ . If $a$ is $\ell$ -connected and $c$ is $(\ell+1)$ -connected, then for every point $x\colon{\mathbin{*}}\to C$ , the induced morphism $\textup{fib}_{x}(f)\to\textup{fib}_{cx}(f^{\prime})$ on fibers is $\ell$ -connected.

We conclude this subsection by recalling the Blakers–Massey and Freudenthal Suspension Theorems in the setting of $\infty$ -topoi.

#### Theorem 4.15 (Blakers–Massey [49, Corollary 4.3.1]).

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -topos and let

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ulcorner} $$

be a pushout square in $\mathcal{X}$ . If $f$ is $k$ -connected and $g$ is $\ell$ -connected, then the induced morphism $A\to B\times_{D}C$ is $(k+\ell)$ -connected.

As in the classical setting, applying the Blakers–Massey Theorem to the pushout defining the suspension immediately implies the Freudenthal Suspension Theorem.

#### Corollary 4.16 (Freudenthal Suspension Theorem).

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -topos, and $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ a pointed $k$ -connected object. Then the unit morphism $X\to\Omega\Sigma X$ is $2k$ -connected.

### 4.2. The infinite James and Hilton–Milnor Splittings

We now explain how to use a connectedness argument to show that if $X$ is a pointed $0$ -connected object of an $\infty$ -topos, then the comparison morphism

$$ c_{X}\colon\bigvee_{i=1}^{\infty}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\to\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X $$

introduced in Notation 2.12 is an equivalence (Proposition 4.18). The James Splitting gives us access to generalized Hopf invariants in this very general setting, and implies the stable Snaith Splitting for $\Omega\Sigma X$ [80]. We also prove the infinite version of the Hilton–Milnor Splitting (Example 4.22). Using Morel’s unstable $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -connectivity Theorem, we explain why these infinite splittings hold in motivic spaces over a perfect field (Corollary 4.24). As an application, we give a new description of $\Omega\Sigma^{2}(\mathbf{P}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,1,\infty\})$ (Example 4.25).

The key tool to prove all of these results is the following lemma about how infinite James Splittings interact with localizations.

#### Lemma 4.17.

Let $\mathcal{Y}$ be an $\infty$ -category, $j\colon\mathcal{X}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{Y}$ a full subcategory, and assume that the inclusion $j$ admits a left adjoint $L\colon\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{X}$ . Assume that:

- (4.17.1) The $\infty$ -categories $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ have universal pushouts and the $\infty$ -category $\mathcal{Y}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ has countable coproducts.

- (4.17.2) The functor $L\colon\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{X}$ commutes with finite products and the formation of loop objects (e.g. $L$ is left exact).

If $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ is a pointed object with the property that the comparison morphism

$$ c_{j(X)}\colon\bigvee_{i\geq 1}\Sigma_{\mathcal{Y}}j(X)^{\wedge i}\to\Sigma_{\mathcal{Y}}\Omega_{\mathcal{Y}}\Sigma_{\mathcal{Y}}j(X) $$

is an equivalence in $\mathcal{Y}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ , then the comparison morphism

$$ c_{X}\colon\bigvee_{i\geq 1}\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}}X^{\wedge i}\to\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}}\Omega_{\mathcal{X}}\Sigma_{\mathcal{X}}X $$

is an equivalence in $\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ .

#### Proof.

Since the localization $L\colon\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{X}$ preserves the terminal object, the functor $L$ descends to the level of pointed objects. Moreover, since $L$ preserves finite products, the functor $L\colon\mathcal{Y}_{{\mathbin{*}}}\to\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ commutes with smash products. Since the functor $L\colon\mathcal{Y}_{{\mathbin{*}}}\to\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ also commutes with the formation of loop objects, we see that the morphism $c_{X}$ is equivalent to $L(c_{j(X)})$ . The assumption that the morphism $c_{j(X)}$ is an equivalence completes the proof. ∎

#### Proposition 4.18 (James Splitting).

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -topos. Then for each $0$ -connected pointed object $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ , the natural comparison morphism

$$ c_{X}\colon\bigvee_{i\geq 1}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\to\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X $$

is an equivalence in $\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ .

#### Proof.

Since every $\infty$ -topos is a left exact localization of a presheaf $\infty$ -topos and presheaf $\infty$ -topoi are hypercomplete (see Definition 4.8), by Lemma 4.17 we are reduced to the case that $\mathcal{X}$ is hypercomplete. That is, it suffices to show that the morphism $c_{X}$ is $\infty$ -connected.

To see this, notice that for each integer $n\geq 1$ , the summand inclusions of $\bigvee_{i=1}^{n}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}$ into $\bigvee_{i=1}^{\infty}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}$ and

$$ \Sigma\Omega\Sigma X\simeq\left(\bigvee_{1\leq i\leq n}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\right)\vee(X^{\wedge n}\wedge\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X) $$

(Corollary 2.11) fit into a commutative triangle

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bigvee_{i=1}^{n}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bigvee_{i=1}^{\infty}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c_{X}} $$

Since $X$ is $0$ -connected, combining (4.12.1), (4.12.4), (4.12.5) and Corollary 4.16 we see that $X^{\wedge n}\wedge\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X$ is $n$ -connected. Hence (4.12.2) shows that the summand inclusion

$$ \bigvee_{i=1}^{n}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\to\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X $$

is $(n-1)$ -connected. Similarly, since $X$ is $0$ -connected, combining (4.12.1), (4.12.5), and Corollary 4.11 we see that the object $\bigvee_{i\geq n+1}^{\infty}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}$ is $(n+1)$ -connected. Again applying (4.12.2), we see that the summand inclusion

$$ \bigvee_{i=1}^{n}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\to\bigvee_{i=1}^{\infty}\Sigma X^{\wedge i} $$

is $n$ -connected. The commutativity of the triangle (4.19) combined with (4.10.5) show that the morphism

$$ c_{X}\colon\bigvee_{i\geq 1}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\to\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X $$

is $(n-1)$ -connected. Since this is true for each integer $n\geq 1$ , we have shown that morphism $c_{X}$ is $\infty$ -connected, as desired. ∎

#### Remark 4.20.

Of course, in the proof of Proposition 4.18 we can further reduce to the case $\mathcal{X}=\mathbf{Spc}$ and the claim follows from the classical James Splitting. The purpose of our proof is to provide an explaination that does not appeal to the classical result but, rather, only uses basic manipulations available in an $\infty$ -topos.

#### Proposition 4.21 (Hilton–Milnor Splitting, general version).

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with universal pushouts and countable coproducts, and let $X,Y\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ be pointed objects.

- (4.21.1) If the comparison morphism $c_{Y}$ is an equivalence, then there is a natural equivalence of pointed objects

$$ \Omega X\times\Omega\Sigma Y\times\Omega\left(\Sigma\Omega X\wedge\bigvee_{j\geq 1}Y^{\wedge j}\right)\similarrightarrow\Omega(X\vee\Sigma Y)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

- (4.21.2) If the comparison morphisms $c_{X}$ and $c_{Y}$ are equivalences, then there is a natural equivalence of pointed objects

$$ \Omega\Sigma X\times\Omega\Sigma Y\times\Omega\Sigma\left(\bigvee_{i,j\geq 1}X^{\wedge i}\wedge Y^{\wedge j}\right)\similarrightarrow\Omega\Sigma(X\vee Y)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

#### Proof.

For (4.21.1), first note that the Hilton–Milnor Splitting of Theorem 3.1 provides an equivalence

$$ \Omega(X\vee\Sigma Y)\simeq\Omega X\times\Omega\Sigma Y\times\Omega\Sigma(\Omega X\wedge\Omega\Sigma Y)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

The claim now follows from the natural natural equivalences

## 5. The James filtration & metastable EHP sequence

In classical algebraic topology, the metastable EHP sequence is the statement that the composite

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega\Sigma X} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega\Sigma X^{\wedge 2}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{2}} $$

is a fiber sequence in a range depending on the connectedness of $X$ , known as the metastable range. Here the first map $X\to\Omega\Sigma X$ is the unit and $h_{2}$ is the Hopf map (Construction 4.26). For the higher Hopf maps $h_{n}\colon\Omega\Sigma X\to\Omega\Sigma X^{\wedge n}$ , there is an analogous fiber sequence in a range

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega\Sigma X} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega\Sigma X^{\wedge n}\hbox to0.0pt{\ ,\hss}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{n}} $$

where $\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X)$ is the $(n-1)$ st piece of the James filtration on $\Omega\Sigma X$ .

This section is dedicated to a non-computational proof of the metastable EHP sequence in an $\infty$ -topos that only makes use of the Blakers–Massey Theorem and some basic connectedness results (see Theorem 5.19). In §​ 5.1 we review the James filtration. In §​ 5.2 we refine the James Splitting to a splitting

$$ \Sigma\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)\simeq\bigvee_{i=1}^{n}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

In §​ 5.3, we give our non-computational proof of the metastable EHP sequence via the Blakers–Massey Theorem, and also record a computational proof for posterity.

### 5.1. The James filtration

Classically, the James filtration $\{\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)\}_{n\geq 0}$ provides a multiplicative filtration on the free monoid $\mathrm{J}(X)$ on a pointed space $X$ , in the homotopical sense. At the point-set level, $\mathrm{J}(X)$ can be presented as the free topological monoid on $X$ , and $\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)$ can be identified the subspace of words of length at most $n$ in $\mathrm{J}(X)$ . Concatenation of words then supplies $\{\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)\}_{n\geq 0}$ with the structure of a filtered monoid. Since the trivial monoid and trivial group coincide, if $X$ is connected, then the free monoid $\mathrm{J}(X)$ on $X$ coincides with the free group $\Omega\Sigma X$ on $X$ .

In a general $\infty$ -category, we can define the James filtration as follows. This definition is provided in [54, Section 3] in the context of homotopy type theory; the arguments made in [54, Section 3] are formal and valid in any $\infty$ -topos.

#### Theorem 5.4 ([54, Section 6]).

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -topos and $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ a pointed object. If $X$ is $0$ -connected, then the morphism $u\colon\mathrm{J}(X)\to\Omega\Sigma X$ is an equivalence.

Brunerie [54] gives an elementary proof of the following connectedness estimate.

#### Lemma 5.5 ([54, Proposition 4]).

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -topos, $k\geq 0$ an integer, and $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ a pointed $k$ -connected object. Then the morphism $i_{n-1}\colon\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X)\to\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)$ is $(n(k+1)-2)$ -connected.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -topos, $k\geq 0$ an integer, and $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ a pointed $k$ -connected object. Then for each integer $n\geq 0$ , the object $\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)$ is $k$ -connected.

#### Proof.

If $n=0$ , then the claim is clear since $\mathrm{J}_{0}(X)={\mathbin{*}}$ . If $n>0$ , then by Lemma 5.5 the morphisms $i_{0},\ldots,i_{n-1}$ are all $(k-1)$ -connected. Hence the basepoint

$$ i_{n-1}\cdots i_{0}\colon{\mathbin{*}}\to\mathrm{J}_{n}(X) $$

is $(k-1)$ -connected; equivalently, $\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)$ is $k$ -connected (4.10.6). ∎

#### Lemma 5.7 ([54, Proposition 6]).

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -topos, $k\geq 0$ an integer, and $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ a pointed $k$ -connected object. Then the morphism $u_{n}\colon\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)\to\Omega\Sigma X$ is $((n+1)(k+1)-2)$ -connected.

### 5.2. Splitting the James filtration

The purpose of this subsection is to prove the following splitting of the James filtration, which we use in our proof of the metastable EHP sequence (Theorem 5.19).

#### Proposition 5.8.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with universal pushouts, and let $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ . Then there is a splitting

$$ \Sigma\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)\simeq\bigvee_{1\leq i\leq n}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

If $\mathcal{X}$ is an $\infty$ -topos and $X$ is $0$ -connected, then under the map $\Sigma u_{n}\colon\Sigma\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)\to\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X$ , the splitting (5.9) is an equivalence onto the first $n$ factors of the splitting $\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X\simeq\bigvee_{i\geq 1}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}$ of Proposition 4.18.

The proof of Proposition 5.8 requires some preliminaries. We need to relate the cofiber of $i_{n}$ to smash powers of $X$ ; before doing so we need some preparatory lemmas.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with finite products and pushouts, and let $X,Y\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ . Then there is a cofiber sequence

where the leftmost vertical map is the coproduct insertion. The cofiber of the coproduct insertion $X\to X\vee Y$ is $Y$ , and the cofiber of the basepoint ${\mathbin{*}}\to X\wedge Y$ is $X\wedge Y$ . To conclude, note that taking vertical cofibers in (5.11) results in a cofiber sequence. ∎

The following is a straightforward application of Lemma 1.13.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with pushouts and a terminal object and let

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with universal pushouts, and let $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ . Then for each integer $n\geq 0$ , there is a natural equivalence

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma(X\times\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)) \displaystyle\simeq\Sigma(X\wedge\mathrm{J}_{n}(X))\vee\Sigma X\vee\Sigma\mathrm{J}_{n}(X) \displaystyle\Sigma\Big(X\times\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X)\operatornamewithlimits{\sqcup}^{\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X)}\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)\Big) \displaystyle\simeq\Sigma(X\wedge\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X))\vee\Sigma X\vee\Sigma\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

Moreover, the left vertical map in (5.17) is induced by the suspensions of the identity on $X$ , identity on $\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)$ , and the map $i_{n}\colon\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X)\to\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)$ . Under the identifications

$$ \Sigma(X\wedge\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X))\simeq X\wedge\Sigma\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X)\text{\qquad and\qquad}\Sigma(X\wedge\mathrm{J}_{n}(X))\simeq X\wedge\Sigma\mathrm{J}_{n}(X) $$

of Lemma 2.26, we see that the map

$$ \operatorname{id}_{X}\wedge r_{n-1}\colon\Sigma(X\wedge\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X))\simeq X\wedge\Sigma\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X)\longrightarrow X\wedge\Sigma\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)\simeq\Sigma(X\wedge\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)) $$

is a retraction of $\Sigma(\operatorname{id}_{X}\wedge i_{n-1})$ . Hence the map

$$ (\operatorname{id}_{X}\wedge r_{n-1})\vee\operatorname{id}\vee\operatorname{id}\colon\Sigma(X\wedge\mathrm{J}_{n}(X))\vee\Sigma X\vee\Sigma\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)\longrightarrow\Sigma(X\wedge\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X))\vee\Sigma X\vee\Sigma\mathrm{J}_{n}(X) $$

supplies the desired retraction of the left vertical map in (5.17). ∎

### 5.3. Proofs of the metastable EHP sequence

In this subsection, we present two proofs of the metastable EHP sequence in the setting of $\infty$ -topoi. Before making a precise statement of the main result, we need the following easy lemma.

#### Lemma 5.18.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -topos, $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ be a pointed $0$ -connected object, and $n\geq 1$ an integer. Then the composite

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega\Sigma X} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega\Sigma X^{\wedge n}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u_{n}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{n}} $$

is null. Here $h_{n}$ is the Hopf map of Construction 4.26.

#### Proof.

It suffices to prove the corresponding statement on adjoints: in other words, we need to show that the composite

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma X^{\wedge n}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma u_{n}} $$

is null. This is an immediate consequence of Proposition 5.8. ∎

We can now state the metastable EHP sequence.

#### Theorem 5.19 (metastable EHP sequence).

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -topos, $k\geq 0$ an integer, and $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ a pointed $k$ -connected object. Then for every integer $n\geq 1$ , the morphism $\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X)\to\textup{fib}(h_{n})$ induced by Lemma 5.18 is $((n+1)(k+1)-3)$ -connected.

#### Remark 5.20.

The metastable EHP sequence for $\infty$ -topoi of hypersheaves on an ordinary site with enough points proven by Asok–Wickelgren–Williams [51, Proposition 3.1.4] is a special case of Theorem 5.19.

The first proof of Theorem 5.19 we present is internal to $\infty$ -topoi, and only uses basic facts about connectedness and the James construction, as well as the Blakers–Massey Theorem. The second reduces to the $\infty$ -topos $\mathbf{Spc}$ of spaces, then uses the homology Whitehead Theorem and Serre spectral sequence to give a calculational proof of the metastable EHP sequence in the classical setting. Both perspectives are valuable, and we present the second here in part because the calculational proof of the metastable EHP sequence does not seem to be easy to locate in the literature.

#### Internal proof of Theorem 5.19.

First we show that it suffices to prove the claim where we replace $\textup{fib}(h_{n})$ by the fiber of the natural morphism $\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)\to X^{\wedge n}$ . Observe that we have a commutative square

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X^{\wedge n}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega\Sigma X} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega\Sigma X^{\wedge n}\hbox to0.0pt{\ ,\hss}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u_{n}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{n}} $$

where the right vertical morphism is the unit. Since $X$ is $k$ -connected, the morphism

$$ u_{n}\colon\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)\to\Omega\Sigma X $$

is $((n+1)(k+1)-2)$ -connected (Lemma 5.7) and $X^{\wedge n}$ is $(n(k+1)-1)$ -connected (4.12.5). By the Freudenthal Suspension Theorem (Corollary 4.16) the unit morphism $X^{\wedge n}\to\Omega\Sigma X^{\wedge n}$ is $2(n(k+1)-1)$ -connected. Since $n\geq 1$ , we have that

$$ 2(n(k+1)-1)\geq(n+1)(k+1)-2\hbox to0.0pt{\ ,\hss} $$

so that both of the vertical morphisms in (5.21) are $((n+1)(k+1)-2)$ -connected. Applying Corollary 4.14 to the square (5.21), we see that the induced morphism on horizontal fibers

$$ \textup{fib}(\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)\to X^{\wedge n})\to\textup{fib}(h_{n}) $$

is $((n+1)(k+1)-3)$ -connected. Therefore, to prove that the morphism $\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X)\to\textup{fib}(h_{n})$ is $((n+1)(k+1)-3)$ -connected, it suffices to show that the induced morphism

$$ \mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X)\to\textup{fib}(\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)\to X^{\wedge n}) $$

is $((n+1)(k+1)-3)$ -connected.

Since $X$ is $k$ -connected, $\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X)$ is $k$ -connected (Corollary 5.6) and the morphism

$$ i_{n-1}\colon\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X)\to\mathrm{J}_{n}(X) $$

is $(n(k+1)-2)$ -connected (Lemma 5.5). Applying the Blakers–Massey Theorem (Theorem 4.15) to the cofiber sequence

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{J}_{n}(X)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbin{*}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X^{\wedge n}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i_{n-1}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ulcorner} $$

provided by Proposition 5.13, we see that morphism (5.22) is $((n+1)(k+1)-3)$ -connected. ∎

#### Computational proof of Theorem 5.19.

Let $m\coloneq(n+1)(k+1)-3$ ; we need to show that the map

$$ \mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X)\to\textup{fib}(h_{n}) $$

is $m$ -connected. The following two facts allow us to reduce to proving the claim in the case that $\mathcal{X}=\mathbf{Spc}$ .

- (1) If the conclusion of Theorem 5.19 holds for the $\infty$ -topos $\mathbf{Spc}$ , then it holds for any presheaf $\infty$ -topos.

- (2) If $L\colon\mathcal{Y}\to\mathcal{X}$ is a left exact left adjoint between $\infty$ -topoi, then $L$ preserves: suspensions, loops, smash products, fibers, the James filtration, and $m$ -connectedness (this last fact is [44, Proposition 6.5.1.16]).

Now we prove the claim for $\mathcal{X}=\mathbf{Spc}$ . The claim is trivial if $n=1$ , so assume that $n\geq 2$ . Since $X$ is $k$ -connected by assumption, the smash power $X^{\wedge n}$ is $(nk+n-1)$ -connected (4.12.5). Since $\Omega\Sigma X^{\wedge n}$ is simply-connected, the Serre spectral sequence for (integral) homology has $\operatorname{E}^{2}$ -page

$$ \operatorname{E}^{2}_{p,q}=\operatorname{H}_{p}(\Omega\Sigma X^{\wedge n};\operatorname{H}_{q}(\textup{fib}(h_{n})))\cong\operatorname{H}_{p}(\Omega\Sigma X^{\wedge n})\otimes\operatorname{H}_{q}(\textup{fib}(h_{n}))\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

Since

$$ \operatorname{H}_{p}(\Omega\Sigma X^{\wedge n})\cong\bigoplus_{i\geq 0}\widetilde{\operatorname{H}}_{p}(X^{\wedge n})^{\otimes i}\hbox to0.0pt{\ ,\hss} $$

and $\widetilde{\operatorname{H}}_{p}(X^{\wedge n})^{\otimes i}$ becomes nontrivial in degree $i(nk+n+2)$ , we find that

$$ \operatorname{H}_{p}(\Omega\Sigma X^{\wedge n})\cong\operatorname{H}_{p}(X^{\wedge n})\text{\qquad for\qquad}p<2(nk+n+2)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

In particular, $\operatorname{E}^{2}_{p,0}=\operatorname{H}_{p}(X^{\wedge n})$ for $p<2(nk+n+2)$ . Consequently, the Serre spectral sequence has no nontrivial differentials off bidegrees $(p,0)$ with $p<2(nk+n+2)$ .

The $\operatorname{E}^{2}$ -page of this spectral sequence is very simple if $p+q<(n+1)(k+1)$ : in this range, $\operatorname{E}^{2}_{p,q}$ vanishes unless one of $p$ or $q$ is zero, in which case

$$ \operatorname{E}^{2}_{p,0}=\operatorname{H}_{p}(X^{\wedge n})\text{\qquad and\qquad}\operatorname{E}^{2}_{0,q}=\operatorname{H}_{q}(\textup{fib}(h_{n})) $$

(note that $(n+1)(k+1)\leq 2(nk+n+2)$ ). Recall that for $p<2(nk+n+2)$ , the Serre spectral sequence has no nontrivial differentials off bidegrees $(p,0)$ . Moreover, for $q<(n+1)(k+1)-1$ , are also no nontrivial differentials with target in bidegree $(0,q)$ . Consequently, for

$$ p+q<(n+1)(k+1)-2\hbox to0.0pt{\ ,\hss} $$

we find that the Serre spectral sequence collapses at the $\operatorname{E}^{2}$ -page, and therefore that

$$ \widetilde{\operatorname{H}}_{\mathbin{*}}(\Omega\Sigma X)\cong\widetilde{\operatorname{H}}_{{\mathbin{*}}}(\textup{fib}(h_{n}))\oplus\widetilde{\operatorname{H}}_{\mathbin{*}}(\Omega\Sigma X^{\wedge n})\text{\qquad for\qquad}{\mathbin{*}}<(n+1)(k+1)-2\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

The map $\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X)\to\textup{fib}(h_{n})$ then induces a homology equivalence in degrees $<(n+1)(k+1)-2$ . We conclude by the homology Whitehead Theorem. ∎

#### Remark 5.23.

In the case that $n=2$ and $\mathcal{X}=\mathbf{Spc}$ , the computational proof of the metastable EHP sequence given here reduces to the proof presented in [51, Proposition 3.1.2].
